Look for the math

Social choice theory studies how to turn many voters' preference ballots (ordered lists of the choices) into one winner or one ranking. Here are four methods, each sensible on its own.

Four ways to count

Plurality: count only first places. Borda count: with n choices, a first place is worth n points, a second n − 1, down to 1 for last. Plurality with elimination: if nobody has a majority of first places, strike out the choice with the fewest and count again. The scores shown are the last round's. Pairwise comparison: every two choices meet head to head, and the one more voters prefer scores 2 (a tie scores 1 each).

Same ballots, different winners

On the page's ballots (7 ABC, 8 BCA, 10 CBA, 4 ACB), plurality elects A, Borda and pairwise elect B, and elimination elects C. With COMAP's Math Club election (press Four winners example) each method elects someone different: A, B, D and C. The logic test checked both. A choice that beats every other head to head, a Condorcet winner, always wins the pairwise count but can lose the others. Arrow's theorem says that no method can satisfy every fairness condition you would like.

Checking the totals

Plurality scores add up to the number of voters. Borda scores add up to the voters times 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2. Pairwise scores add up to n(n − 1): 2 points for each of the n(n−1)/2 meetings. The test confirmed these totals in 3,000 random elections.

A note on the original

The applet's elimination count has a slip: once A has been struck out it stops early, before anyone has a majority. This page counts the way the method is described. In random elections where A survives, the two counts agree.

On the page's ballots, move one voter at a time from the 10 CBA voters to the 8 BCA voters. When does the elimination winner change?
